newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS - Kazakh leader maintains market reform aims.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kazakh leader maintains market reform aims.

text.p: Despite a groundswell of unrest over unpaid salaries and a hard winter ahead, Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev said on Tuesday he aimed to keep the oil-rich republic on the track of market economic reforms.

Nazarbayev, in a "statement to the people" published in the official daily Kazakhstanskaya Pravda, said that by the first half of 1998 at the latest, privatisation and reform of the country's industrial and financial sectors should be over.
He said the "harshest measures" would be used to close down bankrupt enterprises.
The Kazakh leader, president until 2000 with wide-ranging powers, said his government aimed to halve inflation annually in the republic by the end of the decade.

"The annual level of inflation must fall by no less than half," Nazarbayev said. Annual inflation of 2,200 percent for 1993 dropped to 60 percent in 1995. Both the government and western financial institutions predict annual inflation for 1996 at around 30 percent.
Nazarbayev said he aimed to bring down annual inflation to four to six percent by 2000 and establish growth of three to five percent in the same period.
Nazarbayev's words won praise from David Hoelscher, the International Monetary Fund's representative in the Kazakh capital Almaty.
"These targets are certainly consistent with the programmes discussed with the fund (IMF) and in our view they are certainly achievable targets," Hoelscher said.
But trade union leaders, planning a nationwide demonstration across the former Soviet republic next week over unpaid wages and pensions, slammed the government's reform programme.

"The government's actions will not lead to the stabilisation of production or the protection of jobs," Siyazbek Mukashev, leader of Kazakhstan's Federation of Trade Unions, said. "Most of the population are near a danger line," he told reporters.
Unpaid salaries and pensions form the staple of conversation in shops, bus queues and homes across the republic of 17 million.
"It's just getting worse and worse," said Sergei, a mechanic in his forties who has not been paid his $100 monthly salary since June.
Unpaid government debts to neighbouring countries for gas and electricity promise a harsh winter.
Nazarbayev recognises the difficulties. "The non-payments crisis has taken on a chronic and systemic character which affects not only a large number of enterprises but all sectors," he said.
For their part, western investors are also concerned at the outlook for the Kazakh economy, with actual foreign cash flowing into Kazakhstan lagging way behind promised investments.
Kazakhstan's petrodollars are locked up in a tangle of geopolitics surrounding proposed export routes to western and Asian markets from the landlocked republic.
"The investment outlook has changed from high, bright and rosy to below moderate," said Bijan Sepasy, head of the U.S.-Kazakhstan Council group representing American businesses in the republic.
